Here in Wisconsin, we're still in the icy grip of old man winter's bony uncomfortable fingers. I always get antsy around this time of year, especially the last three or so, and I start obsessing over making plans for the upcoming spring and summer, organizing pictures from last year's trips, and obsessively reviewing gear, looking for sales, inventorying what I have, that sort of thing.

Probably the biggest thing I miss from Reddit, are the ability for niche subs to thrive. I had a nice list of outdoors-oriented subs that I'd browse, looking for gear and reading about people's experiences. It was a major factor in my expanding from Car Camping to hiking/dispersed camping activities too. I wish I had a chatroom (IRC or otherwise) to chat hiking and camping topics with people in, share my knowhow, pick people's brains about thoughts I have, even back when I still reddited things didn't move very fast in those subs.

Voat, as interesting a place as it is, lacks a certain critical mass to populate niche boards like that. Sure, I could put some energy into livening up /v/campingandhiking but I'm far more of a commenter than I am an original submitter on sites like these, and I don't really know what I'd do besides poach topics from reddit and link my gear-and-trip blog.

I wish I had gotten into the hiking side of things a decade earlier. if I'd learned about it back in college, I'd definitely have through-hiked one of the scenic trails. Part of what really sparked the hiking interest in me was seeing the outtake reels from a guy's through-hike video documentary. it just looked like a great time, the way a lot of these people were getting along. Coming across that, during a polar vortex, watching them roam a thousand mile trek up the height of the US, it looked awesome. I wanted to be out there doing it. The other thing is that I'd like to be in better shape, but I hate just running in place in a gym. my ADD can't take it for long, doesn't matter what machine I'm doing, I get antsy. I can't focus. and I've gotta stop before I go crazy. But when I'm hiking out in nature? I can go all day long,

The other, other thing, is that I came to the internet as a lad, and the internet I grew up in was a wild frontier. It was an exclusive club, and a place where you could do things that weren't possible anywhere else. a lot of the shine has worn off the internet, and it's rapidly becoming a boring digital mall, heavily monitored, policed, censored, sanitized. And, as a result, I'm really getting back to my roots as an outdoorsman. I hail from an era where, before I was glued to a keyboard, I'd disappear on my bike all day, not turn back up till dark. I'd spend most of that outside, running amok. If Civilization has come to the internet, I want to be back outside where it's wild again.

Sorry if this was a bit rambly, If you're itchin to get outside, or if you just wanna hear more about what drives me to get outdoors, I'd love to discuss.

I've been camping since the first year I was alive (parents taking me with them on camping trips), and while I primarily car/motorcycle camp I've gotten in my fair share of hiking and kayaking camping trips. I'm really not up on current gear as I bought the best I could find/afford back in the mid 1990's and haven't needed to replace anything. But gear isn't the hard part, IMHO, keeping food interesting is.

I love winter, snoeshoeing opens up hiking to a Completely new level. Though I also love skiing (both alpine/downhill and cross-country). All options make winter not just bearable, but Enjoyable. If you haven't considered it, maybe you should. :)

Pretty much anything really, yeah.

I'm really more of a The-other-three-seasons guy for my outdoors stuff these days. Ski accident left me with some metal in my left leg that gets nice and achy in prolonged frigid temperatures. I miss getting out and skiing, but I've been lacking for a partner, and would be taking a lot of lodge time too. I did pick up some swedish military surplus snow shows the other week, in hopes that I'd feel less trapped indoors if I got out on those.

I've got a lot of pre-modern gear as well, but most of it is Car Camping grade stuff. I do have an eeearly 90s coleman backpacker's stove somewhere, but I haven't found it. That's okay though, I've got stoves galore for some reason.

I'd be curious to hear more about your 90s gear though. What sort of stuff do you take hiking? what pack weight do you aim for?

Tent is a Sierra Designs 3-person (the Flashlight is the most similar current design, 2 pole, mine is a front opening), which is really more like a 2-person plus a little personal gear. I bought it for the pack size, fit perfectly across the back seat and saddle bags of the motorcycle I had at the time.

I'm still sleeping on an original Thermarest long pad and in a ~30deg North Face down bag, though I had to add a 40deg bag when I moved to the SE from the Rockies and sold off a -20deg back at the same time.

Stove is an MSR canister unit like their current Superfly and I have a small assortment of pots that change depending on if I'm soloing overnight, or group camping for a week.

Backpack is a Gregory something or other, I even forget the size... that was bought mostly because I'm 6'4" (not all legs) and it was one of a very few that would go long enough to fit my torso. I like that it also has a 3l water bladder.

Then I have other crap I've bought and sometimes use, like a UV steri-pen for water treatment, a ton of waterproof bags from small aloksaks (think high tech ziplock) up through a rather large Watershed brand duffel bag (ideal for motorcycle use). All sorts of paracord trinkets I've made over the years, a handful of whistles, compasses, bells, some crazy car-camping stuff like cast iron personal pie cookers (vintage, they were passed down from my grandparents through my parents), and these Amazingly good collapsible forks (for hotdogs and the like). About the highest tech thing I use is a high end LED headlamp and pocket flashlight. Even my knife is just my normal every-day-carry Leatherman (I keep it very sharp, have even removed the serrations on the second blade so it could be sharpened too) that I've been humping around for about 15 years.

I tried using a GPS once, but it was more annoying than anything. I vastly prefer a compass and a map (probably because I know how to use them). The only other thing I sometimes take that uses electricity is my digital camera. No phones, music players, speakers, whatever and I won't camp (well, beyond car camping) with anyone who insists on them.

Sorry about your leg. I spent some time with a 10" plate and 11 screws holding my lower left together too. Thankfully I was just a kid (13) and it didn't hinder my desire for skiing. Snoeshoeing is VASTLY easier on the body, my wife is missing her right knee ACL (with the same "weather leg" issues as you) and loves to snoeshoe. One other thing that made a big difference for her were tights, and I'm talking performance compression gear like CW-X brand stuff not just stretchy pants. Kinda costly to get into at about $100/pair, but they do make a world of difference when it comes to all-day muscle use and limiting fatigue.

Nice! I picked up a 2014 Gregory Baltoro 65(Large) pack and I Love it. Lived out of it for a month on the west coast the same summer I got it, and I've been lugging it up and down sections of the Ice Age Trail since. I bet they'd look like distant cousins, our bags. I saw a video of early "lightweight" b ackpacking gear out of the 90s, and the guy had a gregory bag that looked like a flamboyant primitive ancestor of mine. Is the bladder on yours built-in, or a sleeve for you to hang whatever hydration pack you want like mine has?

I was looking at the MSR Cannister Stoves, and I'm sure they're great stoves, but I saw the $6 chinese canister stoves on amazon, and decided "what the heck, I'll get one of these and if it's terrible, well, I've spent more on fast food in a meal than I wasted on it" and it has turned out to be an awesome little piece of gear. Probably the best price-to-performance ratio of my kit. I also made one of those cat can stoves so I could write about it in my blog, and it's a bit heavier, but I picked up a biolite stove after hearing about people recharging their phones in new york after a hurricane, using them. Sadly, I've been really disappointed in the charge rate on the thing. Better to use it to feed a battery pack and bank up the charge, than directly charge the phone with it.

Water filtration wise, I started with the MSR Sweetwater system, because I really liked how complete the process was, and I didn't mind the idea of pumping. Thing is, even though the water I was filtering wasn't that bad, even though I bought the paper prefilter attachment, it'd get to the point where it'd need to be cleaned (and take about .5l clean water to clean) every 1.5 liters of water or so. Not really ideal when you've been hiking all day, running low on water, and the filter decides to fight you. Might've been okay with a cartridge switch, but that was only like, ~20 liters into that cartridge. Thankfully, REI is great about returns, and I traded in for a Katadyn Gravity Camp bag based filter. I've been loving that. clips right into my camelbak.

Like you, I prefer a compass and a map for navigation, mostly, I just don't trust my phone to have signal AND battery life at any given time. Compass can't run out of batteries. I will use my phone as a camera though, if I don't feel like bringing the good one with me.

I've got a titanium plate and two screws at the knee, and one more screw down at the ankle. I tumbled in some rough garbage at the bottom of the hill, and my left ski didn't detach, became a lever. I'll have to look into that compression gear, I could use something like that. Also been trying to think of a way I could attach a pocket or something so that I could affix one of those disposable handwarmers to the side of my knee, keep some of the cold at bay.
